overlay.caption: sleep stores the day's learning · sleep refills alertness

explain.summary: Two things happened to Chloe. First, memory: the brain strengthens what you've learned while you sleep, so the facts she crammed on Thursday, followed by only three hours of sleep, were stored far less well than Wednesday's, which had a full night. Second, alertness: with so little sleep she reacts more slowly and loses focus. Teens need about 8–10 hours a night.
rules: Studying is stored better the closer she gets to a full night's sleep (8–10 hours).
With a full night, about 95% is stored; with almost none, about a third — the 40% gap reported in sleep studies.
Facts recalled = what she studied × how much was stored; Wednesday's facts had a full night.
Alertness falls with each hour of sleep she's short, more after several short nights in a row.

source.fact: Teens aged 13–18 should get 8 to 10 hours of sleep per 24 hours.
People kept awake all night before learning remembered new images 19% worse on average, and up to 40% worse, than well-rested people.
During a night of sleep some memories are strengthened; you can't pull an all-nighter and still learn effectively.
Sleep-deficient people react more slowly, make more mistakes and have trouble focusing.

choice.what: Storage rises in a straight line up to her full sleep need
choice.why: Real memory gains aren't even across the night; a straight line shows 'more sleep, more stored'.

choice.what: About 10 facts per hour of studying
choice.why: A teaching number so the recall output is countable.

choice.what: Short nights in a row add 25% each to the alertness drop
choice.why: Sleep loss builds up, but by how much differs a lot between people.

choice.what: Age nudges sleep need up for younger teens
choice.why: Need varies within the 8–10 hour range; this is a simple way to show it.

illustrative: Chloe's hours, the 10-facts-per-hour rate and the 0–10 alertness scale are made up for a fictional story.
provenance.studying: Exactly how the sleeping brain chooses which memories to strengthen is still an active research question.

citations.title: Sleep in Middle and High School Students
citations.supports: Teens aged 13–18 should get 8 to 10 hours of sleep per 24 hours (American Academy of Sleep Medicine); about 7 in 10 high schoolers don't get enough on school nights; short sleep is linked to attention problems.

citations.title: Study shows importance of sleep for optimal memory functioning
citations.supports: People kept awake all night before learning remembered new images on average 19% worse two days later, and as much as 40% worse, than well-rested people (Walker lab, Nature Neuroscience).

citations.title: Sleep On It
citations.supports: Sleep researchers explain that during a night of sleep some memories are strengthened, and that you can't pull an all-nighter and still learn effectively.

citations.title: Sleep Deprivation and Deficiency: How Sleep Affects Your Health
citations.supports: During sleep the brain forms pathways to learn and remember; sleep-deficient people react more slowly, make more mistakes and have trouble focusing; ongoing sleep deficiency can weaken the body's defence against common infections.

limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: If you often can't sleep or feel exhausted every day, talk with an adult you trust.
